title: INDUCTION: Finite-Structure Concept Synthesis in First-Order Logic
claim: Allowing larger formula-size budgets raises accuracy for some models but saturates early for others, so model strategies differ and rankings shift.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, left-to-right, dashed vertical budget markers
description: A single line chart titled 'FullObs v1: Budgeted Accuracy Curves'. The x-axis is the AST budget (Δ = pred − gold) from 0 to 100, and the y-axis is accuracy in % from 0 to 60. Fourteen colored curves, one per model, are listed in a legend at lower right: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, Grok4, Gemini 3.5f, Opus 4.6, DeepSeek4Pro, Gemini 3.1, Gemini 3, Grok4.1f, Grok4.3, DSR, Opus 4.5, Hermes4 and GPT-4o. Grok4 in blue is highest, rising from about 40% to about 51%. GPT-5.4 climbs steadily from about 25% to 42%. GPT-5.2 starts near 11% and rises steeply to about 36%. Many weaker models are flat. Gray dashed vertical lines mark 'gold', '+10' and '+25' budgets. The eye goes first to the top blue curve and to the crossing curves in the middle.
caption: FullObs v1 budgeted accuracy curves: Acc@(+$\Delta$) for $\Delta \in [0, 100]$.
abstract: We introduce INDUCTION, a benchmark for finite structure concept synthesis in first order logic. Given small finite relational worlds with extensionally labeled target predicates, models must output a single first order logical formula that explains the target uniformly across worlds, with correctness verified via exact model checking. The benchmark includes three regimes, FullObs, CI (contrastive), and EC (existential completion), nd penalizes formula bloat. We find sharp difficulty gradients, persistent hard structural families, and observe that low bloat formulas generalize far better on held out worlds. Elite recent models show qualitatively different behaviors across tasks and performance metrics, hinting to their different strategies of concept generalization.
